question: What is the main goal of food production when we look at it from a public health point of view?

options.B: Maximizing financial profit for food manufacturers
options.C: Transforming raw natural resources into safe, consumable food
options.D: Eliminating all forms of agriculture globally

explanation: At its core, food production is all about turning what we harvest from nature into safe, nourishing meals for everyone. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to understand the basics of where our food comes from?

options.A: Many chronic health issues and nutritional deficiencies originate in the food system
options.B: Nurses are required to inspect commercial farms daily
options.C: Hospital kitchens are managed directly by nursing staff
options.D: Nurses must calculate the exact cost of groceries for patients

explanation: You'll see many patients dealing with malnutrition or diet-related illnesses, and tracing it back starts with understanding how food is grown and processed. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h1)

question: What is the main reason farmers use crop rotation in their fields?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any water source
options.B: Restoring soil fertility and breaking pest cycles
options.C: Ensuring that only one crop grows forever in a field
options.D: Increasing the retail price of vegetables

explanation: Rotating different crops is a smart farming trick. It gives the soil a break to regain nutrients and confuses pests so they don't take over! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h2)

question: What is one big problem with planting the exact same crop over and over again on a massive scale (monoculture)?

options.A: It automatically stops all rainfall in the region
options.B: It can deplete specific soil nutrients and attract pests
options.C: It completely prevents any food from growing
options.D: It causes crops to turn poisonous to humans

explanation: Growing just one type of plant drains certain minerals right out of the dirt and sends out an open invitation to pests that love that specific plant. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h2)

question: In livestock farming, what do we call a disease that can jump between animals and humans?

options.A: A plant infection caused by heavy rainfall
options.B: A mechanical failure of milking equipment
options.C: An illness that can spread between animals and humans
options.D: A vitamin deficiency found only in farm workers

explanation: Zoonotic diseases are infections that naturally pass from animals to us. Think of illnesses like bird flu or rabies! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h3)

question: Why should we worry when livestock farmers use antibiotics too frequently?

options.A: It causes animals to stop producing milk entirely
options.B: It can contribute to antimicrobial resistance
options.C: It turns the meat a bright green color
options.D: It makes the meat taste bitter to consumers

explanation: Overusing antibiotics on animals creates tougher, resistant germs that can eventually spread to humans and shrug off our best medications. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h3)

question: What is the main goal behind food processing and preservation?

options.A: Ensuring food spoils within twenty-four hours
options.B: Removing all nutrients from vegetables intentionally
options.C: Making food shelf-stable, palatable, and safe
options.D: Making groceries more expensive to buy

explanation: Preservation is all about helping food last longer on the shelf while keeping it tasty and free from nasty germs. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h4)

question: How can eating a lot of heavily processed foods affect a patient's health over time?

options.A: They cause immediate paralysis in the limbs
options.B: They often contain excess sodium, sugar, and unhealthy additives
options.C: They prevent the body from digesting water
options.D: They automatically carry dangerous viral infections

explanation: Heavy processing often sneaks in loads of salt, sugar, and preservatives which are big drivers of chronic conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h4)

question: Which of these is a common biological hazard you might find in contaminated food?
explanation: Harmful bacteria and other living microorganisms are biological hazards responsible for most cases of food poisoning. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h5)

question: Why is keeping a strict eye on temperature so important when storing and transporting food?

options.A: To prevent harmful bacteria from multiplying rapidly
options.B: To make sure the food freezes into solid ice
options.C: To change the natural color of the product
options.D: To eliminate the need for any chemical testing

explanation: Proper temperature control keeps food out of the 'danger zone' where bacteria love to multiply and spoil your meals. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h5)

question: What is the main job of a 'cold chain' logistics system when moving food around?

options.A: Perishable items from spoiling by maintaining low temperatures
options.B: Dry grains from getting wet during heavy rain
options.D: Metal cans from rusting inside storage warehouses

explanation: A cold chain keeps a continuous refrigerator system going from the farm all the way to the store shelf so perishables stay fresh. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h6)

question: What usually happens right away to a community when its food supply chain breaks down?

options.A: Lower rates of chronic illness among residents
options.B: The permanent closure of all local hospitals
options.C: An immediate surplus of fresh vegetables in every market
options.D: Food scarcity and sudden price inflation

explanation: When transport and supply routes fail, food becomes hard to find, and whatever is left usually shoots up in price. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h6)

question: What is the core idea behind sustainable food production?

options.A: Producing as much chemical waste as possible
options.B: Relying entirely on non-renewable fossil fuels
options.C: Growing only luxury crops for export
options.D: Feeding current populations without harming future resources

explanation: Sustainability is about striking a balance: feeding everyone today while taking care of the earth so tomorrow's generations can farm too. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h7)

question: How does climate change directly throw a wrench into farming and crop production?

options.A: Through erratic rainfall, droughts, and rising temperatures
options.B: By making all soils permanently rich and fertile
options.C: Through the complete elimination of all plant pests
options.D: By lowering the global demand for food

explanation: Unpredictable weather, sudden dry spells, and scorching heat mess up traditional planting seasons and ruin harvests. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h7)

question: Which of these is a key thing nurses can do to help with food security?

options.A: Inspecting commercial food processing plants for bacteria
options.B: Operating heavy harvesting machinery on local farms
options.C: Manufacturing nutritional supplements in hospital labs
options.D: Screening patients for hunger and connecting them with resources

explanation: Nurses look out for the whole patient. Asking about food access and linking struggling families to community support programs makes a huge difference. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h8)

question: Why is advocating for good patient nutrition such a big deal in modern nursing?

options.A: Nurses are required by law to cook meals for every patient
options.B: It generates extra revenue for the hospital administration
options.C: Proper nutrition is essential for preventing and managing chronic diseases
options.D: It replaces the need for administering prescribed medications

explanation: Good food is medicine! Helping patients get the right nutrients speeds up their healing and keeps chronic illnesses under control. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T024#GNS227_U2_T024_h8)
